name: Abed-Nego/Azariah
title: Judean and Faithful Witness at the Babylonian Court
summary: Azariah (Hebrew: 'The Lord helps') was a young Judean of royal or noble lineage who was taken captive to Babylon during King Nebuchadnezzar's first deportation around 605 B.C. He received the Babylonian name Abednego (likely a distortion of 'Abed-Nebo', 'servant of the god Nebo') as part of the court's assimilation program. Along with Daniel, Hananiah (Shadrach) and Mishael (Meshach), he was chosen for training and service at the royal court, where the four distinguished themselves through God-given wisdom and insight. Azariah held an administrative position in the province of Babylon. He is above all known for his unwavering loyalty to the God of Israel when, together with Hananiah and Mishael, he refused to worship Nebuchadnezzar's golden image and was thrown into the blazing furnace – yet miraculously saved. The account of the three men in the fiery furnace has throughout history served as a powerful testimony to integrity and reverence for God amid the pressures of exile, demonstrating how faith in God can endure even under life-threatening persecution.
relatedPersons: Hananiah, son of Zerubbabel, descendant of David

keyEvents.title: Exile to Babylon
keyEvents.description: Azariah was taken as a young man from Judah to Babylon and selected for service at King Nebuchadnezzar's court because of his abilities and royal or noble background.

keyEvents.title: Refused to Eat the King's Food
keyEvents.description: Daniel took the initiative so that the four young men would not defile themselves with the king's food and drink. Azariah joined Daniel, Hananiah, and Mishael in this, choosing instead vegetables and water—a test period that showed they were healthier than the others.

keyEvents.title: Received Wisdom from God
keyEvents.description: God gave the four young men – Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah – knowledge and understanding in all literature and wisdom. They were found ten times wiser than all the magicians and enchanters in the entire kingdom.

keyEvents.title: Appointed as Administrators in Babylon
keyEvents.description: After Daniel interpreted Nebuchadnezzar's dream, he asked the king to appoint Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego over the administration of the province of Babylon, which the king granted.

keyEvents.title: Refused to Worship the Golden Image
keyEvents.description: When King Nebuchadnezzar set up a golden image on the plain of Dura and commanded everyone to worship it, Azariah and his two friends Hananiah and Mishael refused to bow down, even under threat of being thrown into the blazing furnace. They declared that their God could save them, but that they would not worship the image regardless.

keyEvents.title: Saved from the Fiery Furnace
keyEvents.description: Azariah, Hananiah, and Mishael were thrown into the blazing furnace, which had been heated seven times hotter than usual. To the king's astonishment, he saw four figures walking freely in the fire – the fourth looked 'like a son of the gods.' The three came out unharmed; not even their hair was singed, their clothes were untouched, and there was no smell of smoke on them.

keyEvents.title: Promoted After the Miracle
keyEvents.description: After the miracle in the fiery furnace, Nebuchadnezzar praised the God of Azariah, Hananiah, and Mishael and promoted them to even higher positions in the province of Babylon.

versions.summary: Azariah was a young Jew of royal or noble descent who was taken captive to Babylon during King Nebuchadnezzar's first deportation. He received the Babylonian name Abednego and served at the Babylonian court alongside Daniel, Hananiah, and Mishael. He is best known for his unwavering faith when he refused to worship King Nebuchadnezzar's golden image and was thrown into the fiery furnace, but was saved by God.
versions.title: The Faithful One in the Fiery Furnace
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'The Faithful One in the Fiery Furnace' is usable but could be more precise. Azariah was also one of Daniel's three friends and an official at the Babylonian court. A title such as 'One of the Three Faithful Ones in the Fiery Furnace' or 'Judean and Official at the Babylonian Court' would have provided a broader picture.; [major] The roles 'servant' and 'wise man' are incomplete. Azariah was an official/administrator in the province of Babylon (Dan 2:49, 3:30). He was also one of the court's chosen ones and could be described as a 'courtier' or 'official'. 'Witness of faith' or 'confessor' would also have been appropriate given his central role in the fiery furnace account.; [minor] In the event 'Received wisdom from God', Azariah is mentioned as one of 'his three friends', but there were four in total (Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah). The text should clarify that it was four young men who received wisdom, and that Daniel additionally received the ability to interpret visions and dreams.; [minor] The event 'Refused to eat the king's food' traditionally focuses most on Daniel as the initiator (Dan 1:8). Azariah's role here is as one of the four who participated, but it was Daniel who 'resolved' not to defile himself. The description should reflect this more clearly.; [minor] In the event 'Delivered from the fiery furnace', it is described that 'God sent his angel', but the text in Dan 3:25 says that Nebuchadnezzar saw a fourth figure who was 'like a son of the gods'. This is a theological nuance – the text does not explicitly identify an angel until verse 28. The description should be more faithful to the text.; [minor] The summary is good but could have included that Azariah received an administrative position in Babylon (Dan 2:49) already before the fiery furnace episode, and that his Babylonian name Abednego probably means 'servant of Nebo' (a Babylonian god), which stands in contrast to his Hebrew name Azariah meaning 'the Lord helps'.; [major] Footnotes are completely missing. There should be added footnotes about the meanings of names (Azariah = 'the Lord helps', Abednego = likely a distortion of 'Abed-Nebo', 'servant of Nebo'), the historical context for Nebuchadnezzar's deportation (605 BC), and archaeological findings related to the Babylonian court.; [minor] There is missing an event about the appointment in Dan 2:49 where Daniel asks the king that Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego be placed over the administration of the province of Babylon, which happens before the fiery furnace episode in chapter 3.

versions.reason: [minor] The role of 'wise man' can be discussed. The text in Daniel 1:17-20 describes that the four received knowledge and insight, but it is Daniel who specifically excels as a dream interpreter. For Azariah, 'wise man' is acceptable based on Dan 1:20, but one might consider whether 'scholar' is more precise.; [minor] In the description of refusing the king's food, it is primarily Daniel who takes the initiative (Dan 1:8). Azariah is not specifically mentioned as the initiator, but he participated. The description is correct in specifying that Daniel took the initiative.; [minor] The summary is good and theologically sound, but the last sentence is somewhat general. It could be strengthened by including Azariah's lasting service at the court and the context of faithfulness in exile.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew name Azariah (עֲזַרְיָה, Azarjah) means 'the Lord helps' or 'the Lord has helped.' This is a theophoric name containing the divine name YHWH, reflecting the parents' faith in the God of Israel.

The Babylonian name Abednego (עֲבֵד נְגוֹ) is likely a distortion of 'Abed-Nebo,' meaning 'servant of Nebo.' Nebo (Nabu) was the Babylonian god of wisdom and writing. The name change was part of a deliberate Babylonian strategy to assimilate the deported Jews into Babylonian culture and religion.

The first deportation to Babylon took place in 605 BC when Nebuchadnezzar defeated Egypt at Carchemish. Babylonian chronicles confirm Nebuchadnezzar's campaign against Judah during this period. The young men who were selected likely belonged to the Jewish elite, consistent with Assyrian-Babylonian practices aimed at securing loyalty from conquered peoples.

The furnace described in Daniel 3 has parallels to known archaeological finds of large brick-burning kilns in Mesopotamia. Such furnaces were used both for industrial purposes and, in some cases, as a method of execution. Babylonian texts testify that fire punishment was a known penalty in the Neo-Babylonian Empire.

The golden image that Nebuchadnezzar set up on the plain of Dura (Dan 3:1) was likely either an image of the king himself or of the god Marduk/Nabu. The plain of Dura has been tentatively identified with Tell Der, about 10 km southeast of Babylon. The command to worship the image may have served as a test of political loyalty just as much as a religious act.

In Jewish and Christian tradition, the three men in the furnace have been seen as examples of faithfulness under persecution. In the additions to Daniel (deuterocanonical/apocryphal writings), there are 'Azariah's Prayer' and 'The Song of the Three Young Men,' which expand the narrative with prayers and praise inside the furnace.

The fourth figure in the furnace (Dan 3:25) is described by Nebuchadnezzar as 'like a son of the gods' (bar elahin in Aramaic). In Christian theology, this has often been interpreted as a Christophany (a revelation of Christ before his incarnation), while Jewish tradition typically identifies the figure as an angel.

The practice of renaming young captives from conquered peoples is well documented in Mesopotamian sources. By giving them new names linked to Babylonian gods, the court sought to break the youths' ties to their original identity and religion and bind them to the Babylonian pantheon and state power.
